title: VMware vSphere: Virtualization Fundamentals and Recovery

questions.question: What is the primary role of an ESXi host?
options: Replace every guest operating system’s filesystem
Provide ONTAP storage-controller failover
Run virtual machines and manage their access to physical compute, memory, networking, and storage
Act only as the centralized inventory database
questions.explanation: ESXi is the hypervisor layer. Distinguish it from vCenter management, the guest OS, external storage, and application services when tracing a problem.

questions.question: How do vCenter Server and vSphere differ conceptually?
options: vCenter is the same thing as a VMFS datastore
vCenter is the guest OS installed in every VM
vCenter is a centralized management component within the broader vSphere platform
vSphere is only a physical network switch
questions.explanation: vCenter manages inventory and cluster operations across hosts. vSphere refers to the broader virtualization platform rather than one running guest VM.

questions.question: What is a useful purpose of VMware Tools or an appropriate supported open-vm-tools installation?
options: Replace the guest’s application backups
Provide guest integration, drivers/services, and management capabilities
Provide a license for every application inside the VM
Make every storage path redundant
questions.explanation: Guest integration supports operations such as guest status, graceful shutdown, and relevant drivers or services. It does not establish application availability or replace backups.

questions.question: Does assigning four vCPUs normally dedicate four physical CPU cores to a VM?
options: No; virtual CPUs are scheduled on available physical execution resources
Yes, and other VMs cannot use any idle capacity
Yes, each vCPU always owns one physical core exclusively
Only if the VM uses thin-provisioned disks
questions.explanation: vCPU allocation describes the virtual machine’s CPU configuration. Scheduling, reservations, limits, contention, and host hardware determine its actual resource experience.

questions.question: What is a datastore in vSphere?
options: A Fibre Channel initiator WWPN
A logical storage container used for VM files and related objects
A CPU scheduling reservation
A guest operating system’s drive letter
questions.explanation: Datastores can use different backing technologies, such as VMFS on block devices or NFS file storage. A datastore and an individual guest virtual disk are different layers.

questions.question: Which interpretation of these illustrative VM files is correct?
options: Deleting any .vmdk is a safe way to remove unused RAM
The .vmx is configuration; the .vmdk files describe or contain virtual-disk data
The .vmx is always the independent backup of the guest disk
The .vmdk is a physical FC switch configuration
questions.explanation: Understand VM configuration and virtual-disk files before investigating storage. Disk descriptors, backing extents, and snapshot chains are related; do not manually delete unfamiliar files.
questions.code:
Illustrative VM directory:
app01.vmx
app01.vmdk
app01-flat.vmdk

questions.question: Which pairing correctly distinguishes typical VMFS and NFS datastores?
options: VMFS is a backup format; NFS is a CPU scheduler
Both require ESXi to format an NFS export as VMFS
NFS is always a guest-local disk; VMFS is always a remote file share
VMFS uses block storage; NFS mounts a file service from a server
questions.explanation: VMFS means Virtual Machine File System and typically uses block devices supplied through FC or iSCSI. An NFS datastore instead consumes an exported filesystem. Protocol and filesystem layers matter when tracing storage connectivity.

questions.question: A NetApp-backed VMFS datastore uses iSCSI. Which sequence represents its storage dependency chain?
options: VM files → VMFS → presented LUN → iSCSI paths → storage system
VMFS → NFS export policy → FC zoning only
Guest hostname → snapshot name → ESXi CPU reservation
VM files → SMB user account → vCenter database → guest pagefile
questions.explanation: Map the actual protocol path before troubleshooting. Access controls, sessions, LUN presentation, host discovery, and multipathing are separate links in the chain.

questions.question: What is an important risk of thin-provisioned virtual disks?
options: Their future growth can exceed available datastore capacity if physical headroom is not managed
They cannot store database files
They make guest free space identical to datastore free space
They allocate their entire configured capacity immediately in every case
questions.explanation: Logical provisioning is not the same as consumed or available physical space. Monitor both the guest and backing datastore, including snapshots and competing workloads.

questions.question: Why is a VMware VM snapshot not a sufficient independent backup?
options: A snapshot never records any changed blocks
VM snapshots are always stored at a different site
Its delta chain depends on the VM’s underlying virtual disks and storage
A snapshot guarantees database transaction consistency
questions.explanation: A snapshot provides a dependent point-in-time rollback mechanism. Use an appropriate backup workflow with recoverable copies and restore validation rather than retaining snapshots as the backup strategy.

questions.question: What is the safe approach to removing an unwanted VM snapshot?
options: Delete delta files directly from the datastore browser
Use supported snapshot deletion/consolidation operations and monitor space and I/O
Rename the base VMDK until the snapshot disappears
Disconnect the datastore while the VM is writing
questions.explanation: Deletion/consolidation merges required disk changes through supported workflows. Manual file removal can break the disk chain and destroy access to VM data.

questions.question: What is a key consequence of reverting a VM to an earlier snapshot?
options: The guest always retains every later database transaction
Changes made after the snapshot can be lost from the restored state
The snapshot is converted into an offsite backup automatically
All other VMs in the cluster revert at the same time
questions.explanation: Rollback has data-consistency and service consequences. Confirm the intended recovery point, dependencies, approvals, and application-specific recovery requirements first.

questions.question: What is the usual distinction between a template and a clone?
options: A template is a SAN path; a clone is an Ethernet port
A template is a provisioning source; a clone is a new VM copy created from a source
Templates automatically remain patched without maintenance
A clone always shares the same hostname and IP safely
questions.explanation: Provisioning also requires identity customization, network settings, access controls, patching, and backup enrollment. A copied VM is not automatically production-ready.

questions.question: After an ESXi host fails, what does correctly configured vSphere HA normally attempt for protected VMs?
options: Restart them on eligible surviving hosts with access to required resources
Restore all guest files from the latest backup automatically
Live-migrate their running memory out of the already-failed host
Guarantee that applications experience no interruption
questions.explanation: High Availability (HA) recovery includes failure detection, placement, VM restart, and application startup. Eligibility, capacity, storage access, and policy affect the outcome; HA is not a zero-downtime guarantee.

questions.question: What is the primary purpose of compute vMotion?
options: Recover memory from a host that has already lost power
Copy all datastores to an independent backup repository
Move a running VM’s execution to another compatible host with minimal interruption
Replace every application’s failover mechanism
questions.explanation: vMotion is primarily a planned live-migration capability. It relies on a functioning source and suitable destination connectivity, compatibility, and resources.

questions.question: What does Storage vMotion primarily change?
options: The backing storage location of a VM’s files or virtual disks
The physical location of the entire storage array
The database schema inside the guest
The VM’s application-level replication topology
questions.explanation: Storage migration and compute migration address different layers. Review compatibility, free capacity, workload impact, and the chosen migration operation’s requirements.

questions.question: What is DRS primarily responsible for?
options: Recovering deleted guest files
VM placement and resource balancing within a cluster, using migration when appropriate
Implementing RAID parity for every datastore
Making all physical network links use the same VLAN
questions.explanation: DRS stands for Distributed Resource Scheduler. Distinguish its placement and balancing role from HA recovery and from vMotion as the migration mechanism.

questions.question: Why can HA admission control block powering on another VM even when some host capacity appears free?
options: It always reserves an entire datastore for every VM
It only checks whether the VM name is unique
It rejects all VMs without snapshots
It preserves capacity needed to meet the configured failover policy
questions.explanation: Failover readiness requires usable spare resources, not only current utilization. Review the policy and reservations rather than disable protection merely to clear a warning.

questions.question: If vCenter becomes unavailable while ESXi hosts remain healthy, what normally happens to already-running VMs?
options: They all power off immediately
Every VM moves to a public cloud
They continue running, although centralized management and some operations are affected
Their guest disks become read-only automatically
questions.explanation: The data plane is not identical to the centralized management plane. An existing HA configuration can still provide host-level protection, but management-dependent operations and recovery details need separate assessment.

questions.question: What is a strong readiness check before migrating a production VM?
options: Confirm only that both hosts answer a management ping
Make the VM’s IP address match vCenter’s address
Remove all reservations and security settings without review
Verify compatible compute, required networks and storage access, resources, and supported migration prerequisites
questions.explanation: Exact requirements depend on the migration type and versions. Use the compatibility check and current supported procedure rather than relying on one remembered prerequisite.

questions.question: What is EVC intended to provide within its supported scope?
options: A common exposed CPU feature baseline to support migration compatibility
Extra physical CPU cores for every VM
A replacement for checking virtual-device compatibility
Automatic migration between any Intel and AMD processors
questions.explanation: Enhanced vMotion Compatibility addresses CPU feature exposure. It does not make arbitrary hardware combinations or every migration scenario compatible.

questions.question: What should normally happen before planned work requiring an ESXi host outage?
options: Evacuate or safely stop affected workloads and verify the maintenance plan and remaining capacity
Assume entering maintenance mode creates backups
Disable HA permanently on every cluster
Unplug storage links to force evacuation
questions.explanation: Maintenance mode is part of a controlled workflow, not proof of readiness. Consider placement constraints, local storage, dependent services, and whether surviving hosts can support the workload.

questions.question: Which description correctly distinguishes reservation, limit, and shares?
options: Reservation is a guaranteed minimum when admitted; limit is a cap; shares express relative priority under contention
All three always dedicate exclusive hardware
Reservation is only a label; limit is a minimum; shares add physical memory
Shares guarantee a fixed CPU percentage at all times
questions.explanation: Resource controls affect scheduling and entitlement in different ways. Poorly chosen reservations or limits can affect admission, utilization, and performance.

questions.question: A VM is ballooning or host-swapping even though its host appears to have free memory. Which setting should you inspect?
options: The alphabetical order of its datastore name
Only the VM’s DNS search suffix
An artificially low memory limit on the VM
Whether its template was stored on NFS
questions.explanation: A configured limit can constrain the VM independently of overall host free memory. Correlate VM settings, guest demand, and reclamation metrics before adding resources or migrating.

questions.question: What does CPU ready time measure conceptually?
options: The percentage of physical memory reserved for vCenter
Time the guest application is actively using a disk
Time a virtual CPU is ready to execute but is waiting to be scheduled
Time before a VM snapshot finishes deleting
questions.explanation: Low average CPU utilization does not rule out scheduling contention. Interpret the metric’s scope and interval rather than apply an unexplained universal threshold.
questions.code:
Illustrative observation:
Guest CPU utilization is moderate.
CPU ready time rises during the slowdown.

questions.question: How does guest ballooning differ from hypervisor swapping?
options: Ballooning adds physical RAM; swapping adds vCPUs
Ballooning uses a guest driver to reclaim memory; hypervisor swapping moves guest memory pages to host-managed storage
Both are the same as an application backup
Hypervisor swapping always proves the guest has no free cache
questions.explanation: They are different reclamation mechanisms with different implications. Inspect host pressure, VM limits, guest behavior, and actual swap activity before choosing a remedy.

questions.question: Why can adding many vCPUs to a slow VM fail to improve performance?
options: Every application scales linearly with CPU count
vCPUs always provide unlimited dedicated physical cores
The workload may not use them effectively and scheduling or NUMA effects can worsen
Adding vCPUs removes storage latency automatically
questions.explanation: Right-size from measured demand and workload behavior. More virtual hardware is not a substitute for identifying CPU scheduling, memory, storage, network, or application bottlenecks.

questions.question: Why does vSphere HA use more than a single management-network symptom to assess host availability?
options: The guest DNS resolver alone determines the HA primary
Any lost ping proves every VM has powered off
Datastore heartbeats are application transaction logs
Network isolation and actual host failure need to be distinguished using available evidence
questions.explanation: Management heartbeats and datastore heartbeating can help interpret failures. Recovery behavior also depends on isolation response, storage conditions, and configuration.

questions.question: What is a VMkernel network adapter typically used for?
options: A guest’s virtual Ethernet adapter in every case
The configuration file of a virtual disk
Only the physical switch’s out-of-band management
Host services such as management, vMotion, or IP storage
questions.explanation: Distinguish vmk interfaces used by host services from guest vNICs and physical uplinks such as vmnic adapters. Each belongs to a different part of the network path.

questions.question: What is a key management distinction between a standard switch and a distributed switch?
options: A distributed switch automatically makes all VLANs reachable
A standard switch is configured per host; a distributed switch provides centralized switch configuration across participating hosts
A distributed switch replaces the physical upstream network
A standard switch carries only storage traffic
questions.explanation: Centralized configuration simplifies consistency, but physical connectivity and correct host participation still matter. The virtual switch does not replace the physical network fabric.

questions.question: A VM is connected to the intended VLAN-tagged port group but cannot reach its gateway. What should you verify next?
options: That the VM has a recent snapshot
The VLAN’s end-to-end physical uplink/trunk path and the guest’s IP configuration
That vCenter and the guest have the same hostname
Only that the datastore has free space
questions.explanation: A port-group setting is only one part of connectivity. Check guest settings, virtual port placement, uplinks, physical switch VLAN allowance, and the gateway path.

questions.question: Why is NIC teaming not a complete replacement for iSCSI multipathing?
options: Link redundancy and storage-session/path management operate at different layers
Multipathing configures physical switch VLANs automatically
NIC teaming grants LUN access through igroups automatically
Either feature guarantees storage availability without other configuration
questions.explanation: A supported design must align VMkernel interfaces, network topology, initiator sessions, and storage path policies. Do not assume one redundancy feature covers every failure mode.

questions.question: What is generally true if vCenter is unavailable but hosts and existing distributed-switch connections remain healthy?
options: Existing host-side forwarding can continue, while changes and some port-allocation operations are affected
The distributed switch becomes a physical switch
All future reconnections and moves are guaranteed to work without vCenter
Every VM immediately loses all network traffic
questions.explanation: Existing forwarding and management/configuration operations are different. VM reconnection or recovery can depend on port binding and configuration, so avoid treating vCenter independence as universal.

questions.question: What does this command specifically help test?
options: Successful guest database authentication
Whether the NFS export grants write permission
The validity of every vMotion compatibility requirement
IP reachability from the chosen VMkernel interface to the peer address
questions.explanation: Testing the relevant host interface is more useful than only pinging from a workstation. A successful ping still does not prove MTU, storage authorization, or every service requirement.

questions.question: Why must a jumbo-frame design be checked end to end rather than only at the VMkernel interface?
options: An MTU setting automatically changes every physical switch
Inconsistent MTU along the path can break or fragment traffic despite matching endpoints
Every storage protocol requires jumbo frames to function
Jumbo frames replace the need for routing
questions.explanation: Check the relevant interfaces and physical path using supported tests. Jumbo frames are a design choice, not a universal prerequisite for all storage connectivity.

questions.question: What does this read-only command help investigate?
options: The number of snapshots in every VM
The guest’s current Windows drive letters
Available storage-device paths and their reported states
Only NFS user permissions
questions.explanation: Use path information to correlate a failed datastore with host, adapter, fabric, and array evidence. A path listing is not a command to format or repair storage.

questions.question: Which question can this read-only command help answer?
options: Which FC zones are configured on the physical switch
Whether every guest has a valid domain login
Which database transactions are committed
Which filesystems/datastores the host reports and whether they are mounted
questions.explanation: Host-visible filesystem information helps scope datastore accessibility and capacity. Compare it with other hosts and storage evidence before attempting recovery actions.

questions.question: What does this command inspect?
options: The list of every application TCP connection inside each guest
The contents of the vCenter database
Physical NIC inventory and reported link-related information
NFS export-policy identities
questions.explanation: Physical link and adapter health are part of the host’s network path. A link-up indication alone does not establish correct VLANs, MTU, routing, or application reachability.

questions.question: What is the focus of this command?
options: Active storage snapshots on ONTAP
Virtual disks attached to every guest
Only physical Fibre Channel ports
The host’s VMkernel network interfaces
questions.explanation: VMkernel interfaces are host networking constructs. Inspect their service association and network path when investigating management, vMotion, or IP-storage connectivity.

questions.question: Why start with a version/build check before using a procedure remembered from five years ago?
options: Because checking a version automatically patches the host
Because the host build number proves backups are valid
Because all releases use identical prerequisites
To select the applicable support, compatibility, and command guidance
questions.explanation: Core concepts endure, but support status, known issues, hardware compatibility, and procedures change. Match guidance to the actual platform and build.

questions.question: Why is esxtop useful during a shared VM performance incident?
options: It replaces application and storage-array evidence completely
It only displays the current VMware license key
It exposes host-level compute, memory, storage, and network observations
It automatically repairs every resource bottleneck
questions.explanation: Use host metrics to correlate symptoms and isolate layers, not as an automatic diagnosis. Time alignment and comparisons with healthy workloads make the observations more useful.

questions.question: A nearly full datastore has VMs with growing snapshot deltas. What is the strongest response?
options: Assess impact, growth, free headroom, and supported consolidation or capacity recovery before changing files
Delete the largest delta VMDK manually
Assume guest free disk space proves the datastore is safe
Power-cycle every VM before collecting evidence
questions.explanation: Snapshot growth can exhaust shared storage and affect several workloads. Coordinate backup and storage teams, preserve disk-chain integrity, and validate applications after mitigation.

questions.question: For the same measurement scope, what does the relationship shown here help distinguish?
options: Storage-device/path latency from host-kernel latency in the observed I/O time
Network packet loss from DNS lookup time
Snapshot size from physical free space
Guest CPU ready time from application response time
questions.explanation: DAVG includes the device-driver-to-storage round trip; KAVG reflects host-kernel latency. Correlate these with array and fabric evidence instead of equating every slow I/O with a disk failure.
questions.code:
Illustrative esxtop latency relationship:
GAVG ≈ DAVG + KAVG
DAVG = 4 ms
KAVG = 2 ms
GAVG ≈ 6 ms

questions.question: What is the basic distinction between APD and PDL?
options: APD is always a guest CPU problem; PDL is always low RAM
Both conditions prove the device was intentionally deleted by an administrator
APD means all paths are unavailable without definitive permanent-loss signaling; PDL indicates permanent device loss
They both mean the datastore is full
questions.explanation: All Paths Down and Permanent Device Loss have different detection and recovery implications. Assess the cause and supported HA/storage behavior rather than blindly rebooting or removing devices.

questions.question: What is the right basis for choosing a storage path-selection policy?
options: Assume every active path has identical access characteristics
Always force the same policy on every storage device
Choose the policy with the shortest name
The supported array, protocol, host version, and vendor interoperability guidance
questions.explanation: Supported multipathing behavior depends on the storage implementation. Verify the exact design instead of applying a remembered Round Robin or preferred-path rule universally.

questions.question: What should a production ESXi patch plan include beyond downloading the patch?
options: Only checking that the patch filename contains the current year
Hardware/driver/firmware compatibility, cluster capacity, backups, evacuation, rollback considerations, and validation
Assuming a VM snapshot can roll back every host change
Disabling all monitoring so no alerts are created
questions.explanation: Use the supported lifecycle procedure and change plan. A successful installation task is not the same as validated service recovery or a tested rollback path.

questions.question: Why inspect DNS and time synchronization in a vSphere management or authentication problem?
options: They determine the parity layout of every datastore
A correct DNS record proves the storage fabric is healthy
They directly allocate more vCPUs
Name resolution and time-sensitive identity/services can depend on them
questions.explanation: Management availability depends on several infrastructure services. Check the exact failing operation and its dependencies rather than conclude that credentials alone explain every login issue.

questions.question: What does this PowerCLI pipeline do?
options: Create a new snapshot named PowerState
Change app01’s CPU count
Power on app01 automatically
Read the named VM and display selected identity/state properties
questions.explanation: Get-VM and Select-Object here are inspection operations. Distinguish a read-only query from commands that change power state, configuration, or storage.

questions.question: What does this pipeline inventory, and what does its result not establish?
options: Every file inside each guest
VM snapshots; not the existence of independent recoverable backups
All offsite backup copies and their tested restore times
Only encrypted VMs that cannot be backed up
questions.explanation: Snapshot inventory is useful for lifecycle and capacity review. It is not evidence that backup jobs produced independent, application-consistent, tested recovery copies.

questions.question: An HA restart brings a critical university application VM online after host failure. What should you do before declaring full recovery?
options: Validate application/database dependencies and user workflows, then monitor and investigate the host failure
Assume the application met its RTO because HA was enabled
Skip communication because the recovery was automatic
Close the incident as soon as PowerState is PoweredOn
questions.explanation: Infrastructure recovery and service recovery are different. Confirm representative transactions and dependencies, communicate with the service owner, and preserve evidence for the root-cause investigation.

questions.question: The ESXi host acting as the vSphere HA primary fails. What should the surviving HA agents normally do if they can communicate?
options: Wait indefinitely for an administrator to promote the vCenter appliance to ESXi primary
Elect another primary and continue evaluating protected VMs for recovery
Restart every VM on every surviving host merely because the primary changed
Disable all shared datastores until the failed host returns
questions.explanation: The HA primary is an elected host-agent role, not a fixed vCenter role. Losing it requires another election. VM recovery still depends on the affected workloads, storage access, eligible hosts and resources; a primary change alone does not require restarting unaffected VMs.

questions.question: What does this communication pattern most directly suggest in a traditional, non-vSAN vSphere HA cluster?
options: A mandatory vCenter database restore because all hosts are powered off
A datastore-capacity failure because each group contains two hosts
A normal vMotion operation that guarantees every VM has moved
A network partition between two groups, rather than proof that all four hosts have failed
questions.explanation: A partition separates groups that can still communicate internally. An isolated host has lost HA peer connectivity and uses isolation detection to assess its situation. Correlate datastore heartbeats and agent evidence; do not declare hosts dead from a broken inter-group network path alone.
questions.code:
Illustrative HA network observations:
Host A <-> Host B: reachable
Host C <-> Host D: reachable
A/B <-> C/D: unreachable
All four hosts remain powered on

questions.question: In a non-vSAN cluster, a host stops sending HA network heartbeats but continues updating its selected shared-datastore heartbeat. What does that evidence support?
options: The host may still be running despite a network problem; distinguish partition or isolation from host failure
The host must be powered off because network heartbeats are the only usable evidence
Every guest application on the host has passed a functional health check
Every VM on that host can safely be powered on simultaneously elsewhere
questions.explanation: Datastore heartbeating gives HA another observation when its normal network path is lost. It helps classify the host state, but it neither validates application transactions nor grants permission to create duplicate running VM instances.

questions.question: Why would this configuration explain a VM staying powered on during a confirmed host-isolation event?
options: The same setting necessarily disables VM restart after a physical host failure
HA must live-migrate the VM before applying any isolation response
The effective isolation response tells HA not to shut down or power off that VM for isolation
Reachable storage guarantees that the VM still has a working client network
questions.explanation: Isolation response is a configurable action and may have per-VM overrides. A disabled response can leave a VM running even when its network is unusable. Host isolation, host failure and datastore failure are separate conditions with separate recovery considerations.
questions.code:
Illustrative effective VM settings:
VM: app01
HA restart priority: Medium
Host isolation response: Disabled

questions.question: After an HA network change, agents repeatedly lose contact. Why inspect this log as part of the investigation?
options: It is the guest OS log used to diagnose database service startup
It contains FDM agent evidence about HA communication, elections and protection activity
It replaces testing HA network reachability because every HA issue is a local agent fault
It supplies the complete component-vote layout of every vSAN virtual disk
questions.explanation: FDM is the host-side HA agent. Correlate its timestamps with host health and network changes, including the required HA traffic between hosts. Reading a log provides evidence; it does not by itself fix an HA configuration or network fault.

questions.question: In a supported two-node or stretched vSAN design, what is the witness primarily for?
options: Keeping an independent full backup of every guest virtual disk
Running a third production copy of every protected application VM
Replacing the need for data components on the storage hosts
Hosting witness metadata and participating in object-quorum decisions
questions.explanation: Witness components contribute to quorum without storing the production data blocks. A witness is therefore neither a backup repository nor a substitute for an accessible data replica.

questions.question: For this simplified mirrored object, which surviving set satisfies both the stated vote majority and availability of a full data copy? Assume the displayed votes do not change.
options: Data component A plus the witness
The witness alone
Data component A alone
The vCenter appliance alone, regardless of accessible components
questions.explanation: Two of the three shown votes exceed half, and A supplies a complete data copy. This is an object-level exercise, not a rule that each host always has one vote. Actual component votes and supported failure behavior depend on layout, version and failure sequence.
questions.code:
Illustrative object layout:
Data component A: complete mirror, 1 vote
Data component B: complete mirror, 1 vote
Witness: metadata only, 1 vote
Data component B becomes unavailable

questions.question: HA agents are healthy, but a VM cannot access a vSAN object that has lost quorum. Why is another HA primary election not a complete remedy?
options: The HA primary automatically contains a backup of every vSAN object
A new HA primary can ignore all object-consistency checks without affecting data
HA restart coordination cannot recreate missing storage quorum or an accessible complete data set
Healthy HA agents prove every vSAN component is available
questions.explanation: Compute recovery and storage-object availability are different layers. Investigate the affected object, component reachability, failures and resynchronization state. Moving or restarting compute cannot by itself recover inaccessible storage components.

questions.question: A vSAN maintenance pre-check with Ensure accessibility reports that some objects will remain accessible but become noncompliant. What is the best interpretation?
options: The VM storage policy has automatically been changed to tolerate zero failures
The option can preserve access while reducing policy redundancy, so assess additional-failure risk before proceeding
Every reported noncompliant object is necessarily already inaccessible
Every remaining host can be maintained simultaneously because access was checked once
questions.explanation: Ensure accessibility moves only what is needed to keep objects usable; it does not promise full policy compliance. Review the pre-check, capacity and topology. Full data migration has different requirements and may not be possible in every cluster layout.

questions.question: A cluster uses vSAN storage only. Should you expect its vSAN datastore to appear as an ordinary VMFS/NFS datastore-heartbeat target for vSphere HA?
options: Yes; every datastore listed in vCenter is equally eligible for conventional datastore heartbeating
Yes; vSAN witness components automatically become ordinary shared VMFS heartbeat files
No; vSphere HA is unsupported whenever vSAN is enabled
No; vSAN does not serve as that kind of HA heartbeat datastore
questions.explanation: vSAN clusters have specific HA network and isolation design considerations. They cannot use the vSAN datastore as a conventional datastore-heartbeat target. If additional shared VMFS/NFS datastores are present, evaluate them separately rather than assuming one design applies to all storage types.

questions.question: An ESXi host experiences APD on a datastore, but VMs are not automatically terminated and restarted. Which setting makes that behavior plausible?
options: The effective VM Component Protection APD response is Issue Events rather than a power-off-and-restart policy
DRS automation alone controls APD termination, so VMCP settings are irrelevant
A reachable heartbeat datastore proves every other datastore on the host is accessible
HA restart priority alone always overrides the configured APD response
questions.explanation: An Issue Events response reports the condition without itself changing the VM power state. Check the effective cluster policy, VM overrides, timeout state and alternate-host storage access. Enabling HA does not make every datastore failure trigger an identical recovery action.
questions.code:
Illustrative effective protection settings:
Datastore condition: All Paths Down
APD failure response: Issue Events
Affected VM still powered on

questions.question: A shared VMFS datastore works on two ESXi hosts but is inaccessible on a third after a SAN change. What is the strongest next step?
options: Reformat the datastore from the affected host because two hosts can still read it
Delete the datastore from vCenter to force all hosts to rediscover it
Compare the affected host’s device paths, fabric or IP connectivity, and array initiator/LUN presentation with a healthy host
Assume the whole array has lost all disks because one host cannot see the LUN
questions.explanation: The different host outcomes help isolate the fault domain. Correlate the same device identifier across hosts and verify zoning, initiator mapping, masking and paths as appropriate. Do not destroy a working shared filesystem to resolve one host’s visibility issue.
questions.code:
Read-only device-path inspection; replace the placeholder:
esxcli storage core path list -d <device-id>

questions.question: A VM fails to start with a disk-lock error after backup activity. What should you establish before attempting lock recovery?
options: Which lock-related files can be deleted without checking any owner
Which host or process owns the lock and whether the disk is still legitimately open by a running VM or backup proxy
Whether attaching the same disk to another ordinary VM will bypass all locking
Whether formatting the datastore removes only the lock and preserves every file
questions.explanation: A lock can protect a disk that another process is using. Confirm the active owner and backup attachments, then follow the supported recovery procedure. Forcing concurrent access or deleting storage files without that evidence risks data integrity.

questions.question: For IPv4 on a planned 9000-byte vMotion path, small probes succeed but the second probe fails. What should you investigate?
options: Normal behavior: setting an interface MTU to 9000 requires large no-fragment probes to fail
The need to allow fragmentation and treat a fragmented ping as proof of a 9000-byte path
A definitive CPU compatibility failure that can be identified from ICMP payload size alone
A jumbo-frame or MTU inconsistency along the selected VMkernel-to-peer path
questions.explanation: The 8972-byte ICMP payload plus IPv4 and ICMP headers exercises a 9000-byte IP packet with fragmentation disallowed. Verify endpoints and the physical path; small-packet reachability does not establish jumbo-frame support. This example assumes the interface uses the default TCP/IP stack.

questions.question: vmk2 uses the dedicated vMotion TCP/IP stack. What is the purpose of the stack selector in this diagnostic?
options: Test from the vMotion stack’s network context instead of assuming the default stack’s routing applies
Move all guest traffic onto the vMotion VLAN
Change the destination VM’s CPU compatibility level
Convert a standard virtual switch into a distributed switch
questions.explanation: VMkernel service placement and TCP/IP stack selection affect the path being tested. A successful probe from a management interface or another stack does not prove connectivity for the vMotion stack.

questions.question: A live migration completes, but the VM loses guest-network connectivity only on the destination host. What is the best first investigation?
options: Only the vMotion VMkernel subnet because guest packets always use that subnet
Only the VM snapshot count because migration success guarantees the guest network
The destination VM network mapping, VLAN, active uplinks and physical switch path
The source host’s boot disk because destination uplinks cannot affect a migrated VM
questions.explanation: The migration network and the guest network are distinct paths. Successful memory transfer and compatibility checks do not validate every physical VLAN or uplink at the destination. Compare the guest-facing path with a known-good host.

questions.question: On ESXi 7/8, two software-iSCSI VMkernel interfaces use different broadcast domains and IP subnets. Is adding both to one port-binding configuration a universal fix for missing paths?
options: Yes; port binding automatically routes between all VLANs and storage subnets
No; validate the supported topology because software-iSCSI port binding has specific same-subnet and network-placement requirements
Yes; adding more bindings always increases valid paths regardless of topology
No; iSCSI can never use more than one VMkernel interface in any supported design
questions.explanation: Port binding is a particular software-iSCSI design, not a generic path-repair switch. Broadcom documents common broadcast-domain/subnet, virtual-switch and uplink-mapping requirements. Match the host and array design rather than copying bindings from a different topology.

questions.question: An ESXi storage VMkernel interface can ping the NFS server, but its mount request is explicitly denied by the server. What should you check next?
options: Assume export authorization is correct because the server answers ping
Increase MTU immediately because an explicit mount denial always means jumbo-frame loss
Change the VM guest filesystem permissions before checking the host-to-server export access
The export path and server authorization for the actual ESXi client address and intended NFS protocol configuration
questions.explanation: An explicit server denial points toward the export and access configuration, not proof that the server is unreachable. Validate the client source address, exported path, permissions and supported NFS settings. Ping establishes neither mount authorization nor read/write permission.

questions.question: A host fails, and a protected VM does not restart even though other hosts have spare CPU and RAM. What can this rule explain?
options: The remaining hosts may be ineligible because HA must respect the mandatory VM-to-host placement restriction
Every host with free RAM automatically belongs to the named host group
A Must rule is always ignored during HA recovery
The rule means vCenter has reserved a full backup copy of the VM
questions.explanation: A mandatory VM-to-host affinity rule can prevent HA restart when no permitted host is available. Check effective rules, VM overrides, storage access and resources. Free capacity on an ineligible host is not sufficient.

questions.question: After HA recovery, the application VM starts immediately after the database VM powers on, but the database is not ready to accept connections. What does this reveal?
options: Powered On guarantees the database has completed recovery and accepts transactions
HA restart ordering replaces all guest-service health checks
The configured restart condition or ordering does not necessarily prove application-service readiness
The application must use the vMotion network for database traffic
questions.explanation: Infrastructure milestones such as resource allocation, power-on or guest heartbeats are not equivalent to a ready database service. Review dependency conditions and application retry or health mechanisms, then validate a representative transaction.
